records.why: The old text said the experimental P(2 or 5) would be 'close to but not equal to' P(2) + P(5). That is wrong for the same set of rolls: every roll that shows a 2 or a 5 is counted once under 'A or B' and once under A or B, and no roll can be both, so the frequency of '2 or 5' is always exactly the frequency of 2 plus the frequency of 5. I checked with a 30-roll example: 6 twos and 4 fives give 10 rolls that were '2 or 5', so 10/30 = 6/30 + 4/30. What is only approximate is how near each value is to 1/6 and 1/3. Teachers would otherwise tell learners their correct data are 'wrong'.
records.old: Observable indicator 2: in the die experiment, learners record P(2 or 5) as a value close to but not equal to P(2) + P(5) due to sampling variation — check that learners interpret this as 'close to' not 'exactly,' building realistic data-literacy expectations.
records.new: Observable indicator 2: in the die experiment, each pair's frequency of '2 or 5' must equal its frequency of 2 plus its frequency of 5 exactly (one roll shows one face, so no roll is counted twice). Only the comparison with the theoretical values P(2) = P(5) = 1/6 and P(2 or 5) = 1/3 is approximate, because of sampling variation. Check that learners can say which part is exact and which part is 'close to'.
records.group_headline: Die-roll data in Lesson 4: the experimental P(2 or 5) equals P(2) + P(5) exactly in the same data (not just 'close'); wording corrected in 4 places
records.reference: OpenStax, Introductory Statistics (2nd ed.), Chapter 3 Probability Topics (equally likely outcomes, independent and mutually exclusive events, addition and multiplication rules) (addition rule for mutually exclusive events)

records.why: The lesson said each football match IS an independent event, just like a coin toss, and that a streak carries 'zero information'. That overstates it: matches depend on team strength, so a long winning streak can say something about how strong the team is. What is true, and what the gambler's fallacy gets wrong, is that a streak never makes a loss 'due'. The text now treats independence as a model for matches, states the limit of the analogy, and fixes the streak length to the seven wins in the phenomenon (it said 'five-win streak' and 'match six'). Teachers should decide how far to take this with Grade 10 learners.
records.old: Now connect to the phenomenon: 'Back to Gor Mahia. If each football match is an independent event — just like each coin toss — what does their five-win streak tell us about the probability of winning match six?' Wait 15 seconds. Cold-call 3 learners for brief responses.
records.new: Now connect to the phenomenon: 'Back to Gor Mahia. Suppose we model each match as independent, like a coin toss — what does their seven-win streak tell us about the probability of winning match eight?' Wait 15 seconds. Cold-call 3 learners for brief responses. Then state the limit of the coin analogy: 'A coin is truly independent. A real team is only roughly so: a long streak may hint that the team is strong, but it never makes a loss "due".'
records.group_headline: The coin analogy was stated too strongly (matches are only roughly independent: a streak can hint at team strength, but never makes a loss 'due'); limit now stated in Lessons 6-8 and the Final Explanation; 'five-win' corrected to seven
records.reference: OpenStax, Introductory Statistics (2nd ed.), Ch. 3 Probability Topics (independent events); Tversky & Kahneman (1971), 'Belief in the law of small numbers', Psychological Bulletin (the gambler's fallacy)

records.why: Knock-on: Summary Table states independence of matches as a model, with the streak length matching the phenomenon (seven).

On that model the seven-win streak carries zero mathematical information about the probability of winning match eight; a real team's form may hint at its strength, but a streak never makes a loss 'due'.

records.why: The text claimed that real day-to-day rain in Kisumu is independent (chance unchanged by the previous day) and quoted a '~70% historic' figure. Rainfall occurrence is persistent: wet days cluster, so the real chance of two wet days in a row is higher than 0.7 × 0.7 = 0.49. I could not verify the 70% figure either. The phenomenon is kept but now says 0.7 and independence are modelling assumptions. A teacher may substitute a real Kenya Meteorological Department figure.
records.old: A student notices that the probability of rain on any given day in Kisumu during April (historically ~70%) does not change based on whether it rained the day before. This real Kenyan weather context supports understanding of independent events and how probabilities are combined across two trials.
records.new: A student notices that Kisumu has many rainy days in April and wonders whether rain on one day changes the chance of rain on the next. For this unit we use a simple model: the chance of rain on any April day is 0.7 and the days are independent. Real weather is not exactly independent (wet days tend to come in runs), so the model is an approximation; it supports understanding of independent events and how probabilities are combined across two trials.
records.group_headline: Kisumu rain was presented as truly independent day to day with an unverified '~70%' figure; now stated as a modelling assumption (real rain comes in runs)
records.reference: Wilks, Statistical Methods in the Atmospheric Sciences (precipitation occurrence is persistent and modelled with Markov chains); OpenStax, Introductory Statistics, Ch. 3 (independent events)

records.why: Lesson 8 argued that gambling loses because the multiplication rule makes winning several bets in a row unlikely. That is only part of the story: a long chance of losing a combined bet does not by itself make gambling a loss, since the payout could be generous. The reason gambling loses on average is that the expected payout is below the money staked, which is exactly what Lesson 7's stall calculation shows (collects Ksh 3,600, pays out Ksh 1,800 over 180 spins; checked: 180 × 20 = 3,600; 60 wins × 30 = 1,800). The poster argument now uses both.

records.new: (d) a mathematical argument for why gambling is a losing proposition (the multiplication rule shows a bet that needs two things to go right is less likely to win, and the Lesson 7 stall calculation shows that, on average, the stall pays out less than it collects);
records.group_headline: Lesson 8 explained why gambling loses using only the multiplication rule; now also uses the Lesson 7 stall (average payout below money staked), which is the real reason
records.reference: OpenStax, Introductory Statistics (2nd ed.), Ch. 4 Discrete Random Variables (expected value of a game of chance)

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: All calculations are correct and in simplest form, the correct rule is named and used each time, and working is clearly shown.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Most calculations are correct with the correct rule used; there may be one small arithmetic slip or missing step of working.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Several calculations are incorrect, or rules are mixed up (for example adding when events should be multiplied), or working is missing.

value.criterion: Understanding of independence and the gambler's fallacy
value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Clearly explains that each independent event has a fixed probability that past results cannot change, names the gambler's fallacy, and applies it to both the coin and Gor Mahia.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: States that past outcomes do not change future probability and applies it to the coin or the football example, but the explanation is less complete.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Does not reject the idea that a team or coin is 'due', or gives an explanation that is unclear or incorrect.

value.criterion: Understanding of the range of probability and mutually exclusive events
value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Correctly explains that 0 ≤ P ≤ 1, that probabilities of all outcomes sum to 1, and when events are mutually exclusive and when the addition rule can and cannot be used.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Shows the range and the addition rule correctly but gives limited explanation of when the rule does not apply.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Confuses the range of probability or the meaning of mutually exclusive, or cannot say when the addition rule applies.

value.criterion: Connection to the Driving Question and the Kenyan context
value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Combines all four concepts in a coherent argument, explains how independence is compatible with predicting what is likely, uses the Gor Mahia debate, betting advertisements and the stall data accurately, and ends with a thoughtful responsible decision.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Uses most concepts and the Kenyan context correctly, and gives a reasonable conclusion about responsible decisions.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Gives a general answer with few concepts, little or no reference to the Kenyan phenomenon, or no conclusion about decision-making.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Writing is clear, logical and uses correct mathematical vocabulary in full sentences throughout.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Writing is mostly clear with mostly correct vocabulary.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Writing is hard to follow or key vocabulary is missing or misused.

records.why: The CBE scale has four levels (Exceeds, Meets, Approaches, Below Expectations) but the current data contract allows only three level fields, so the 'Below Expectations' level cannot be written into the rubric. Teachers can record it as work that does not reach the 'Approaches' descriptor. The contract owner would need to add a fourth field.

No KICD source for Essential Mathematics is available here: the Grade 10 Mathematics PDF in data/raw/curriculum_pdfs is the Core Mathematics design, so the learning outcomes (a to i), key inquiry question, competencies, values and PCIs could not be checked word for word and were not changed. Differences from the Core text that look worth a check against the Essential design: Core Sub-Strand 3.2 'Probability 1' has 12 lessons and 7 outcomes (this data has 8 lessons and 9 outcomes); the Core key inquiry question is 'How is probability applied in real life situations?' (the data has 'How do we apply probability in day-to-day life?'); the Core PCIs are Social Cohesion, Life Skills and Road Safety (the data has Life Skills and Financial Literacy); Core values are Responsibility and Social Justice (the data has Responsibility and Unity). Strand and sub-strand numbers (3.0 and 3.2) and names match the Core design. All nine outcomes are taught and assessed across Lessons 1 to 8 and the Final Explanation.

records.why: The phenomenon states as fact that during the 2023 Kenyan Premier League season fans and commentators debated whether Gor Mahia's winning streak was 'bound to end soon', and Lesson 1 gives a specific 7-match streak. I cannot verify this. If it is not accurate, label the scenario as illustrative ('imagine a team on a winning streak') or replace it with a real streak the teacher can confirm. Left unchanged because the teachers chose this phenomenon.
